prompt: G2 holds `Wholesale`. What does `=G2="wholesale"` return?
hint: Does a comparison of text look at capital letters?

choices.text: `FALSE`, because the capital W does not match
choices.why: A comparison ignores case. `EXACT` is the function that does not.

choices.text: `TRUE`
choices.why: Right. Excel compares text without regard to case, so the two are the same text.

choices.text: `#VALUE!`, since text cannot be compared with an equals sign
choices.why: Text is compared with `=` all the time; that is how every test of a channel works.

choices.text: `Wholesale`, the value held in the cell
choices.why: A comparison returns a logical value, not the contents of either side.

prompt: Why does `=4<=E2<10` answer `FALSE` even on a row where E2 is 5?
hint: Excel evaluates it left to right, one comparison at a time.

choices.text: Excel cannot compare a cell with two numbers in one formula
choices.why: It can, with `AND`. The chain is accepted; it just means something else.

choices.text: It compares `4<=E2` first, then compares that `TRUE` with 10, and a logical value ranks above every number
choices.why: Right. `TRUE<10` is `FALSE`, so the chain is `FALSE` on every row.

choices.text: 5 is not between 4 and 10 under Excel's rounding rules
choices.why: No rounding happens; 5 is plainly between them. The formula is not asking that question.

choices.text: The formula needs spaces around each operator
choices.why: Spaces change nothing here; Excel reads the same two comparisons either way.

prompt: A column of codes pasted from another system shows `1001` in A2, and `=A2=1001` answers `FALSE`. What is the likely explanation?
hint: Lesson 1 section 08 has met this cell before.

choices.text: The comparison ignores numbers with four digits
choices.why: Nothing about the length of a number changes a comparison.

choices.text: A2 holds the text 1001, and text never equals a number
choices.why: Right. The characters 1, 0, 0, 1 are not the number 1001. Lesson 6 converts such columns.

choices.text: Excel needs quotes around 1001 to compare it
choices.why: Quotes would make it text; then it would match the text in A2, which hides the problem rather than solving it.

choices.text: The cell is formatted to show a value that differs from the one stored
choices.why: A format can round a number, but it does not make 1001 unequal to 1001.

prompt: `=B2>=___(2026,1,1)` is `TRUE` for every sale made on the first of January 2026 or later.
hint: The function that builds a day from a year, a month and a day.

prompt: `=IF(G2="Wholesale",H2,0)` is filled down column J. What does `=SUM(J2:J109)` answer?
hint: The revenue of the wholesale sales, and nothing for the rest.

prompt: Why does `=IF(E2>=4,"Medium",IF(E2>=10,"Large","Small"))` label no sale `Large`?
hint: Follow a sale of 14 bags through it.

choices.text: A sale of 10 bags or more passes `E2>=4` first and stops there
choices.why: Right. The first test that passes decides, so the test for Large is never reached.

choices.text: An IF nested inside another cannot return text
choices.why: It can; this one returns `Medium` and `Small` without trouble.

choices.text: The data holds no sale of 10 bags or more
choices.why: It holds 22. The order of the tests hides them.

choices.text: Excel reads nested tests from the innermost outwards
choices.why: It reads from the outside in, which is exactly why the outer test wins.

prompt: What does `=IF(E2>=10,"Large")` show on a row of 3 bags?
hint: The third argument is missing.

choices.text: An empty cell
choices.why: An empty result needs `""` as the third argument. Without one, IF returns the test's own answer.
That is what IFS gives when no test passes. IF has a default.

choices.text: `FALSE`
choices.why: Right. With no value if false, IF shows `FALSE`, which is rarely what anybody wanted.

choices.text: `Small`, the opposite of Large
choices.why: Excel does not invent an opposite; it only returns what the formula names.

prompt: `=IFS(E2>=10,"Large",E2>=4,"Medium")` has no final `TRUE` pair. What does it show on a row of 2 bags?
hint: What does IFS do when no test passes?

choices.text: `Small`, since that is the only size left
choices.why: IFS knows only the values it was given, and `Small` is not one of them.

choices.text: `FALSE`, as IF does without a third argument
choices.why: That is IF's behaviour. IFS has no value if false at all.
Right. No test passed, so there is nothing to return. A last pair of `TRUE` and a value catches every such row.

choices.text: Nothing, an empty cell
choices.why: IFS never returns an empty cell unless one of its values is `""`.

prompt: Which formula is `TRUE` exactly for the sales of 4 to 9 bags?
hint: A range is two comparisons that must both hold.

choices.why: That chain compares a logical value with 10 and is `FALSE` on every row.
Every number is either at least 4 or under 10, so this is `TRUE` on every row.
That takes 5 to 10 bags: it drops 4 and adds 10.
Right. Both comparisons must hold, and it is `TRUE` on 41 rows.

prompt: A colleague writes `=OR(G2="Wholesale","Shop")` to mark wholesale and shop sales. What is wrong with it?
hint: Read each argument as a question on its own.

choices.text: `Shop` alone asks nothing about G2
choices.why: Right. Each argument must be a whole comparison: `G2="Shop"`.

choices.text: OR accepts only numbers, so text must go in AND
choices.why: OR takes comparisons of any kind; the trouble is that the second argument is not one.

choices.text: The quotes around `Shop` should be removed
choices.why: Without quotes Excel looks for a name `Shop`. The comparison is still missing.

choices.text: Nothing; OR compares G2 with every value listed
choices.why: OR does not distribute G2 over its arguments. That reading is the mistake.

prompt: `=AND(G2="Wholesale",E2<10)` is filled down. On how many rows is it `TRUE`?
hint: Wholesale sales under ten bags.

prompt: Match each function or operator to when it returns `TRUE`.
hint: Every, at least one, the opposite, different.

pairs.right: Every comparison inside it is TRUE
At least one comparison inside it is TRUE

right_distractors: Exactly one comparison inside it is TRUE

prompt: J110 holds `=IFERROR(H110/E110,"")`, and somebody types `5 bags` in E110. What does J110 show?
hint: `5 bags` is text, and text divided gives an error. Then what?

choices.text: `#VALUE!`, which tells you the row needs fixing
choices.why: That is what the plain division would show. IFERROR replaces it.

choices.text: Nothing, exactly as when the row was empty
choices.why: Right. The sale is in the sheet and invisible to the check.

choices.text: 5, because Excel reads the number at the start of the text
choices.why: Excel does not pull numbers out of text in arithmetic.

choices.text: 0, the value IFERROR gives when no value is named
choices.why: Here the value is named: `""`, the empty text.

prompt: `=IFERROR(H2/E2O,0)`, with the letter O, is filled down and shows 0 on every row. What happened?
hint: What does Excel make of `E2O`?

choices.text: E2O is read as E20, so every row divides by the same cell
choices.why: Excel never turns a letter into a digit. It looks for a name instead.

choices.text: Dividing by a cell in another row always gives zero
choices.why: A division by another row's cell gives a number, not zero.

choices.text: IFERROR rounds small results down to zero
choices.why: IFERROR does not round; it replaces errors and leaves values alone.

choices.text: `E2O` is no cell: each division is `#NAME?`, turned into 0
choices.why: Right. A typo became a column of zeros, and nothing in the sheet says so.

prompt: Which formula shows nothing on an empty row 110 and still shows an error when `Bags` holds text?
hint: Test for the case you expect, and let the rest through.

choices.why: It hides the text error too: every error becomes empty.
Right. Only the empty row is caught; `5 bags` still shows `#VALUE!`.
IFNA lets `#DIV/0!` through, so the empty row shows an error.
The IF inside is right, but the IFERROR around it hides the text error again.

prompt: Which errors does `IFNA` replace?
hint: Its name says it.

choices.text: Every error, like IFERROR but faster
choices.why: IFNA is the narrow one. It exists so the other errors stay visible.

choices.text: Only `#N/A`, the error of a value not found
choices.why: Right. Every other error passes through it, which is the point.

choices.text: `#DIV/0!` and `#N/A`, the two expected errors
choices.why: A division by zero passes straight through IFNA.

choices.text: None: it only tests whether a cell is empty
choices.why: Testing for empty is `=E110=""`. IFNA replaces one error.

prompt: K holds the flag `=IF(B2>=DATE(2026,1,1),1,0)`, filled down. What does `=SUM(K2:K109)` answer?
hint: The number of sales made in 2026.

prompt: J holds `=E2>=10` filled down, showing `TRUE` and `FALSE`. What does `=SUM(J2:J109)` answer?
hint: What does SUM do with logical values in a range?

choices.text: 22, one for every `TRUE`
choices.why: That would be true of a column of 1 and 0. SUM skips logical values in a range.

choices.text: `#VALUE!`, because the column is not numbers
choices.why: SUM does not complain about what it skips; that is why the result is believable.
Right. SUM skips logical values in a range, so it adds nothing. `=COUNTIF(J2:J109,TRUE)` answers 22.

choices.text: 108, the number of rows
choices.why: Counting rows is COUNTA's job; SUM adds values and finds none it uses.

prompt: What does `=AVERAGE(J2:J109)` over a column of 1 and 0 tell you?
hint: Ones over rows.

choices.text: The share of rows where the flag is 1
choices.why: Right. For the Big flag it is 0.2037, a fifth of the sales.

choices.text: The number of rows where the flag is 1
choices.why: That is the SUM of the column. The average divides it by the number of rows.

choices.text: The average bags of the flagged sales
choices.why: The flag column holds 1 and 0, not bags, so its average knows nothing about bags.

choices.text: Nothing useful, since averaging a flag mixes two kinds of row
choices.why: Averaging a 1/0 column is exactly how a share is computed.

prompt: J (big) and K (in 2026) hold 1 or 0. Which formula is a flag for a sale that is big or in 2026, or both?
hint: A flag holds 1 or 0, nothing else.

choices.why: A product is 1 only where both are 1: that is AND.
It gives 2 where both are 1, so it is no longer a flag, and summing it counts those sales twice.
Right. The sum is above zero when either is 1, and IF turns that back into 1 or 0.
The second test asks whether K2 is 0, which is the opposite of a sale in 2026.

prompt: `=IF(E2>=10,"Large",IF(E2>=4,"Medium","Small"))` is filled down. How many sales are `Medium`?
hint: Count them, or check that Large, Medium and Small add up to 108.

prompt: Put in order what Excel does with `=IF(E2>=10,"Large",IF(E2>=4,"Medium","Small"))` on a row of 6 bags.
hint: From the outside in.
items: Go to the value if false: the inner IF
trap: The inner IF is never read first; it runs only because the outer test failed.

prompt: Café Serra wants `Review` beside every online sale above R$ 400 of revenue, and nothing elsewhere. Which formula does it?
hint: Two conditions that must both hold, then a label or the empty text.

choices.text: `=IF(OR(G2="Online",H2>400),"Review","")`
choices.why: OR marks every online sale and every big sale of any channel.

choices.text: `=IF(G2="Online",H2>400,"Review")`
choices.why: This puts TRUE or FALSE on online rows and `Review` on all the others: the arguments are in the wrong places.

choices.text: `=AND(G2="Online",H2>400)`
choices.why: It finds the right rows but shows TRUE and FALSE, not the label.

choices.text: `=IF(AND(G2="Online",H2>400),"Review","")`
choices.why: Right. AND joins the two tests, and IF turns the answer into the label or nothing.

prompt: With J holding the Big flag and M2 `=H2*J2` filled down, what does `=SUM(M2:M109)` give, in reais?
hint: The revenue of the sales of ten bags or more.
